title: 1  Sets
text:
1.1 Sets
This chapter is meant to be a quick introduction to sets. It is placed here so that it may be easily referenced.
Sets are a collection objects where there is no ordering. Elements are not repeated or counted. Sets can contain any object, including other sets, or they can be empty. The empty set is denoted by \(\emptyset\) or \(\{\}\) and is sometimes called the null set. Typically we use curly brackets to denote set notation. Thus a set described in enumeration notation as \(\{a,b,c\}\) is a set that contains elements \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). The order of the elements does not matter. Thus \(\{a,b,c\}\) is the same set as \(\{b,c,a\}\) or \(\{b, a, c\}\). If \(d\) were added to this set, we would have a new set \(\{a,b,c,d\}\), which is different from the original set. If \(a\) were added to the original set, we would still have the same set \(\{a,b,c\}\) because \(a\) is already an element of the set. Thus, elements are not repeated or counted in sets.
We will use enumeration notation right away to start describing important elements for this book. Enumeration notation is most often used when all items in a set can be easily described, the set is finite, or when a pattern can be easily inferred. Since easily inferred is subjective, we find it best to be explicit in our descriptions and notations.
Occasionally, set notation is easier than describing a set in English. For example, “the set containing the set that contains a” can be written as \(\{\{a\}\}\), which is easier to read and understand than the English description. This is an example of a set that contains another set. The inner set \(\{a\}\) is an element of the outer set \(\{\{a\}\}\). The inner set \(\{a\}\) contains the element \(a\). Thus, \(a\) is an element of the inner set \(\{a\}\), and the inner set \(\{a\}\) is an element of the outer set \(\{\{a\}\}\).
As some sets are infinite, we need a way to describe them without enumerating all of their elements. Set-builder notation is a way to describe sets by stating the properties that its members must satisfy. For example, the set of all even integers can be described in set-builder notation as \(\{x \mid x \text{ is an even integer}\}\). This can be read as “the set of all \(x\) such that \(x\) is an even integer”. The vertical bar \(|\) can be read as “such that”. In programming we often think of this pipe as an “OR” symbol, but we must think of it differently when it is in set-builder notation. Another example is \(\{w \mid w\) is a list of letters with one letter containing an \(a\}\), which can be read as “the set of all \(w\) such that \(w\) is a list of letters and one of those letters is an \(a\)”. Think of this notation in two pieces. The first piece is the variable \(w\) that represents the elements of the set. The second piece is the condition that describes the properties of the elements of the set. In this case, the condition is that \(w\) is a list of letters and one of those letters is an \(a\). This is not unlike a variable assignment in programming. We are assigning the variable \(w\) to represent the elements of the set, and we are describing the properties of those elements with the condition.
A subset is a collection of the elements of a set. For example, if we have the set \(\{a,b,c\}\), then \(\{a,b\}\) is a subset of \(\{a,b,c\}\) because it contains only elements that are in \(\{a,b,c\}\). We can also say that \(\{a,b,c\}\) is a superset of \(\{a,b\}\) because it contains all the elements of \(\{a,b\}\). The empty set is a subset of every set because it does not contain any elements that are not in any other set. Thus, \(\emptyset\) is a subset of every set. We use the symbol \(\subseteq\) to denote subset and \(\supseteq\) to denote superset. Thus, we can write \(\{a,b\} \subseteq \{a,b,c\}\) and \(\{a,b,c\} \supseteq \{a,b\}\).
When we are new to sets, this new vocabulary and its usage can be overwhelming. It is important to practice using this vocabulary and notation to become comfortable with it. The more you practice, the more natural it will become. We will be using it throughout the book, and thus you will have plenty of opportunities to practice.
The power set of a set is the set of all subsets of that set. For example, the power set of \(\{a,b\}\) is \(\{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a,b\}\}\). The power set of a set with \(n\) elements has \(2^n\) elements. Thus, the power set of a set with 2 elements has \(2^2 = 4\) elements, which we can see in the example above. The power set of a set with 3 elements has \(2^3 = 8\) elements, and so on. The power set of a set is denoted by \(\mathcal{P}(S)\), where \(S\) is the original set. Thus, we can write \(\mathcal{P}(\{a,b\}) = \{\emptyset, \{a\}, \{b\}, \{a,b\}\}\).
The union of two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of all elements that are in \(A\) or in \(B\) (or in both). The union of \(A\) and \(B\) is denoted by \(A \cup B\). For example, if \(A = \{a,b\}\) and \(B = \{b,c\}\), then \(A \cup B = \{a,b,c\}\). Remember that sets do not care about order and duplication.
The intersection of two sets \(A\) and \(B\) is the set of all elements that are in both \(A\) and \(B\). The intersection of \(A\) and \(B\) is denoted by \(A \cap B\). For example, if \(A = \{a,b\}\) and \(B = \{b,c\}\), then \(A \cap B = \{b\}\). It is not uncommon for the intersection of two sets to be the empty set. For example, the intersection of the set of positive integers and the set of negative integers is simply \(\emptyset\).
To get comfortable with these new terms and operators, we must use them. We will be using them throughout the book, and thus you will have plenty of opportunities to practice. The more you practice, the more natural it will become. Occasionally, these concepts will appear as we tackle the material in the following chapters. Most things we talk about in this class are sets, because sets help us talk about collections of objects.

title: 2  Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)
text:
2.1 Alphabets, Strings, and Languages
This chapter discusses strategies for understanding and working with deterministic finite automata (DFAs). We will cover the basics of DFAs, including their definition, how to construct them, and how to use them to recognize languages. The approach here is unique, but it is designed to help developers understand the material in a way that is intuitive and practical, especially for programmers. We will be using a lot of examples and exercises to help practice and solidify our understanding of DFAs. By the end of this chapter, we should have a good grasp of what DFAs are, how they work, and how to use them effectively.
To start thinking about theory of computation, we define a few useful terms. An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. For example, the binary alphabet is \(\Sigma = \{0,1\}\). A string is a finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet. A string is not a set and order matters. Some example strings, using the binary alphabet, are \(1011\) and \(0101\). These are not unlike a string defined with quotation marks in a programming language like C++. We might write "1011" in C++ to represent a string. "1011" is a string that contains 4 characters. In this book, we refer to the characters as symbols, although, at times, the symbols have meaning. '0' is a symbol, an element of an alphabet, but it may also mean the digit 0. In this book, the empty string is denoted by a tilde, ~, and is a string that contains no symbols. We often use empty strings in programming as well. In C++, we might set a string equal to the empty string, denoted by "". A language is a set of strings. The alphabet of the language is the set of symbols that can be used to create the strings in the language. We might have a language that contains all strings of even length. This language contains strings such as "", 00, 11, 0101, and so on. The language of all strings of even length over the binary alphabet can be denoted as \(L = \{w \mid w\) is a binary string of even length\(\}\). This is an example of a language that contains an infinite number of strings. We will be working with languages that contain both finite and infinite numbers of strings. Test understanding of these definitions with the following exercises.
As we continue, we will use these terms, alphabet, string, and language, frequently. Our alphabets are finite sets that define the characters that are allowed in our strings. Our strings are like words; they are an ordered list of characters. Our languages are sets of strings and they will often be infinite sets (having an unbounded number of strings).

title: 2  Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)
text:
2.2 Finite Automata (FA)
Finite automata (FA) are a type of computational model. They are called finite because they have a finite number of states. Automata is generally used to denote a machine and thus, in this text, we will often use the two words interchangably. Automata utilize states as a kind of finite memory. We might say that a FA can be used to determine if an input string is in the language of the machine. We will use some words interchangably at first and then expand their definitions. A machine recognizes a language but many machines may recognize the same language. States are represented using circles and machines are made up of states with transitions between them. In our diagrams, a state with a straight arrow pointing at it (not from another state) is the start state. A state with a double circle is an accept state. We introduce an additional kind of state in this text. It is a special accept state that also halts the machine, the halt and accept state denoted as ha. They can have a halt and reject as well, sometimes synonmous with a null or trap state depending on the type of finite machine we’re using. If the machine ever enters the halt and accept state, it halts and accepts the input string as being in the language of the machine. We’ll add some additional power to the Ramsey Finite Automata (RFAs) presented in this book to align with our notions as programmers as well, but first, let’s give some background on why we use the notation that we do.
In the C++/C base representation, strings are arrays of characters are terminated by the null character. In C++ this is represented as ‘\0’. Thus a string like “hello” is actually stored as an array of 6 characters. One character for ‘h’, ‘e’, ‘l’, ‘l’, and ‘o’ and then one more for the terminating character – null. Thus, we’ll denote detecting the end of a string (and later the end of other things) by using the null character. Thus, we’ll see \0 on some of our transitions to denote that we’ve detected the end of a string. Typically this is non-traditional and finite automata run until they eat all the input symbols, but we find this can be a helpful tool when thinking about these machines as developers.

title: 2  Deterministic Finite Automata (DFAs)
section: 2.3 Traditional Finite Automata vs Ramsey Finite Automata (RFA)
text:
2.3 Traditional Finite Automata vs Ramsey Finite Automata (RFA)
Unlike many of the finite automata presented in this book, a traditional finite automata will not have halt states and it does not typically have an end of string transition. In the real world, many FA will operate continuously (imagine a red light or a vending machine that takes coins). A traditional finite automata can have many accept states. When an automata finishes processing an input string, it will accept if it is in an accept state (state with a double circle), otherwise it will reject the input string. The approach presented in this book is beneficial because it operates more closely to how we program software to operate and it is how the state machines we’ll look at in the future operate. A language that only needs to look at the first symbol of an input string, could immediately halt and accept or halt and reject based on that symbol. If your need does not include processing the whole string, then we do not bother in the model presented in this book, which we label as a Ramsey Finite Automata (RFA) after the author.
Converting between the formats is not difficult. To turn a traditional FA into an RFA, turn every accept state into a normal state. To each of those states (that were accept states), add an end of string transition from that state to the halt and accept state. Converting from an RFA to a traditional FA is a bit more complicated as we must take special care to end in an accept state which does not halt. We turn most states that point at halt and accept into accept states that have transitions to themselves on all inputs. End of string transitions can be converted into free transitions (we will see these in the nondterministic chapter). The main point is that the two models are not that different and we can convert between them with a little bit of work. The RFA model is more convenient for our purposes in this book, but it is important to understand the traditional model as well. Different FA models appear in different places as more powerful tools in certain situations. They can allow us to take some shortcuts in proofs. In addition, many other texts on the subject will use various model, so it can be helpful to understand them to understand their resources or to get assistance from someone who is using another one.
